This bill will implement part of the government's [Job Ready Graduates Package](https://www.dese.gov.au/job-ready) and includes major proposed higher education funding changes, including how the government currently subsidises university tuition costs. If successful in its current form, the bill will decrease the subsidy for most areas of the humanities and social science as well as in engineering, science, surveying, environmental studies and other areas. On the other hand, it will increase the subsidy for most health fields, education, mathematics and other areas. At the same time, the bill will set new maximum student contribution amounts, which means the degree costs for students are going to change significantly. Sometimes, such as in the case of engineering, the changes appear somewhat contradictory: both the subsidy for engineering and the maximum student contribution rate is being reduced. The bill creates 39,000 additional university places by 2023 and 100,000 over ten years, with cheaper degrees in teaching, nursing, and other areas of expected job demand, including a 42% reduction for teaching and languages, 59% for agriculture and maths, and 18% for science and IT. It also establishes a $900 million National Priorities and Industry Linkage Fund, implements Napthine review recommendations on regional and Indigenous student support, and introduces grandfathering to protect current students.

The speaker moved to reject the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it makes university harder and more expensive, with 40% of students facing fee increases up to $14,500 per year and some degrees more than doubling in cost. They claimed the bill cuts billions from universities, fails to address youth unemployment or demand for places, and would reduce funding for teaching engineering, science, and maths by 16–32%, contrary to the government’s stated aims.

The speaker argued the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020 is a tax on students that increases fees—humanities by 113%, law and commerce by 28%, and 40% of students facing fees of $14,500 a year—while cutting university funding, with UWA losing 3–4% revenue, Curtin University $60 million, and 21,000 staff jobs at risk.

The speaker supported the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020 because it implements key Napthine review recommendations, including $160 million in tertiary access payments, guaranteed Commonwealth places for Indigenous regional students, and increased funding for regional universities, but called for the Senate to refer the bill to the Education and Employment Legislation Committee for review due to concerns over rushed, evidence‑poor changes to student fees that disproportionately affect regional students.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it would increase humanities fees by up to 113%, making university unaffordable for low- and middle-income families, disproportionately affecting women and Indigenous Australians, and representing government interference in students' career choices. He called for the bill to go to a Senate inquiry.

Labor opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it would increase student fees, cut Commonwealth funding, shift debt to students, and harm universities, particularly affecting young people in Corangamite and Victoria during COVID-19.

The bill was opposed for redirecting university funding toward STEM at the expense of humanities, arts, commerce and law, and for including a punitive 50 per cent completion rule that removes loan eligibility; the government was urged to delay implementation by at least two years, grandfather existing students' fees, extend the Indigenous eligibility definition to all Indigenous persons, and refer the bill to the Senate Education and Employment Legislation Committee. Specific concerns included a $4,758 per-student shortfall for science degrees, a rise in student contribution share from 42 to 52 per cent, and a predicted 30 per cent increase in suicides among 15- to 24-year-olds over five years due to COVID-19.

The bill makes it harder and more expensive for young Australians to go to university, with 40% of students facing fee increases of up to 113%—including humanities degrees rising from $27,216 to $58,000—while cutting guaranteed university funding by around a billion dollars a year, and the speaker argued this will limit access to humanities education for disadvantaged students and undermine critical thinking skills needed for future jobs.

The bill was opposed for increasing student fees and cutting university funding, with regional students and universities disproportionately affected. Specific criticisms included a $1 billion annual funding cut, a 7% average fee increase, humanities degree fees rising from $27,216 to $58,000, and the exclusion of universities from JobKeeper.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it would double the cost of many degrees, increase the student share of university funding from 42% to 48%, and deter young people from higher education, while advocating for free education funded by taxing billionaires and corporations.

The Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020 was opposed for increasing student fees—with 40% of students facing $14,500 per year—reducing university funding for STEM courses, and disproportionately harming disadvantaged students and those from Western Sydney, while the government provided no additional university places or JobKeeper for university staff.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it cuts $1 billion from universities, raises student fees by up to 113% for humanities, and removes loadings from enabling programs at the University of Newcastle despite its regional campuses in Taree, Moree, Orange, Port Macquarie and Coffs Harbour. They criticised the Morrison government for excluding universities from JobKeeper and warned that 21,000 university jobs face elimination within six months.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment bill, arguing it would cut university funding by around $1 billion per year, increase student fees by an average of 7% (with humanities fees doubling to $58,000), and harm regional universities, women, and First Nations students, citing cuts to per-student funding for engineering (16%), nursing (8%), and teaching (6%).

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it entrenches privilege rather than allowing access based on merit, and criticised cuts of $3 billion from TAFE and a reduction of 140,000 apprentices and trainees under the government.

Andrew Leigh We are now in the greatest economic downturn that Australia has seen since the Great Depression. Research from the Australian Treasury has revealed just how damaging this can be, particularly to young Australians. That research has looked at the so-called scarring effect, the long-term effect, of graduating in the teeth of a recession. I know this effect well, having finished high school in 1990 and seen some of my classmates who searched for work utterly unable to find it at that time. We know now that there are 13 jobseekers for every job vacancy, so this problem is particularly acute. The research conducted by Daniel Andrews of the Australian Treasury—now at the OECD—titled _The career effect of labour market conditions of entry_ found that a person who enters the labour market for the first time during a recession is more likely to be unemployed and more likely to be unemployed for longer. When they do find a job—if they do—they are more likely to work at a low-productivity firm and are less likely to switch firms, thereby missing out on the wage gains that come from that. Their estimate is that somebody who enters the workforce in a year in which youth unemployment is five percentage points higher suffers an eight per cent hit to their earnings in the first year and a 3.5 per cent hit to their earnings in the fifth year. The scarring effect lasts a full decade. We know that in Australia right now we are seeing significant adverse effects right across the labour market. We've seen a downturn in hours of some 20 per cent and the effective unemployment rate, the Treasurer tells us, will go to 13 per cent. The difference between those is JobKeeper, a wage subsidy scheme urged on the government, after they initially dragged their heels, by Labor. Mehreen Faruqi I rise to continue my speech on the Coronavirus Economic Response Package (Jobkeeper Payments) Amendment Bill 2020. Women are already bearing the brunt of the economic impacts of the pandemic—so much so that economists have said that we are in a pink collar recession. Women lost their jobs twice as fast as men when the economy was shut down. Women are over-represented as casual workers and in industries most affected by shutdowns like retail and hospitality. Women are under-represented in the few industries which received targeted stimulus, such as the construction sector. Young women have been forced to dip into their already meagre superannuation balances at disproportionate rates to make it through the crisis, which is going to decimate their retirement savings. The government's approach to early childhood education and care was a double whammy for women and their earning potential. Not only did the government rip away access to free child care—potentially one of the most significant boosts to women's capacity to enter and remain in the workforce in a generation—but it carved the highly feminised early learning and care workforce out of JobKeeper altogether, months before the scheme was originally scheduled to end. There has been no job creation for women during this crisis and there is none planned for the recovery. Instead, women have been totally shafted and left to fend for themselves. I've said it before and I'll say it again: our recovery plans must have women at the front and centre of planning and decision-making. This recovery must be a feminist recovery. The bill would change how Australians with dual citizenship can lose their citizenship for terrorism-related conduct, moving from automatic loss to a decision by the Minister for Home Affairs.

Under the proposed law, the Minister could decide to strip citizenship from a dual national who engages in specified terrorism conduct, fights for a declared terrorist organisation, or is convicted of a terrorism offence and jailed for at least three years.
The bill would also lower the prison sentence threshold from six years to three years and extend the time period for considering such cases back to 29 May 2003.
Replaces the automatic loss of citizenship with a ministerial decision model.
Allows the Minister to revoke a citizenship cessation determination on request or on their own initiative.
Lowers the sentence threshold for citizenship cessation from six years to three years.
Extends the eligibility period for citizenship cessation to include conduct or convictions from 29 May 2003.
Adds transitional provisions for cases where a person lost citizenship without ministerial awareness.
Dual nationals who engage in terrorism-related conduct or are convicted of terrorism offences, and the Minister for Home Affairs who would make the decisions.
